document_check.note: Document is Egas-López, Balogh, Imre, Hoffmann, Szabó, Tóth, Pákáski, Kálmán and Gosztolya (2022), 'Automatic screening of mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease by means of posterior-thresholding hesitation representation', Computer Speech & Language 75:101377. It is a speech study using silent and filled pause (hesitation) features to classify HC, MCI and mild AD. This matches the review's citation of Egas-López et al. 2022 for pause structure in speech as a discriminative signal.

cited_result: The review cites the paper qualitatively: pause structure (silent and filled hesitations) in spontaneous speech is a discriminative signal. The principal result behind that claim is the three-class (HC/MCI/mild AD) linear-SVM classification using Posterior-Thresholding Hesitation Representation features, fused over all three speech tasks (abstract: accuracy 70.7%, F1 89.6, mean AUC 0.804; 25 HC, 25 MCI, 25 mAD).
tool_reason: The cited finding rests on how well a multivariable machine-learning classifier (an SVM on hesitation features) tells diagnostic groups apart, so it is a diagnostic prediction-model performance question.

domains.rationale: Groups were sampled by known diagnosis (a diagnostic case-control design). Participants whose diagnosis was contested were then removed, and the sample was cut down to demographically matched groups. These steps exclude the hard, borderline cases and are likely to inflate discrimination.

signalling.question: 1.1 Were appropriate data sources used (e.g. cohort, RCT or nested case-control data)?
signalling.quote: The recordings were collected from three categories of subjects: those suffering from MCI, those affected by early-stage AD (mild AD or mAD), and those having no cognitive impairment at the time of recording

signalling.question: 1.2 Were all inclusions and exclusions of participants appropriate?
signalling.quote: Due to technical issues like poor sound quality and controversial diagnosis (i.e. when our clinical expert panel could not reach a consensus), some subjects were filtered out. Furthermore, we insisted on performing our experiments on data where the demographic properties of the speaker groups did not differ significantly, which also reduced the number of subjects.

domains.rationale: Every participant had the same three-task recording protocol. Features come automatically from an acoustic DNN trained on a separate corpus. The only manual step was trimming silence at the start and end of each recording, and speech is available at the intended time of use.

signalling.question: 2.1 Were predictors defined and assessed in a similar way for all participants?
signalling.quote: Hence, we had three recordings for each subject, each containing spontaneous speech with a different speaker task; these recordings were not split any further.

signalling.question: 2.2 Were predictor assessments made without knowledge of outcome data?
signalling.quote: Each recording was edited; namely, parts before the subject started to speak and after his last phoneme uttered were manually removed.

signalling.question: 2.3 Are all predictors available at the time the model is intended to be used?
signalling.quote: In a real application scenario (e.g. within a mobile phone application), this step could be automated at the time of recording

domains.rationale: Diagnosis came from an expert-panel consensus using standard criteria (Petersen; McKhann 2011) and cognitive tests, not speech features, and was made before the recordings were analysed. The interval between diagnosis and recording is not reported, which is a minor gap for a cross-sectional diagnostic question.

signalling.question: 3.1 Was the outcome determined appropriately?
signalling.quote: Diagnosis was based on the consensus of a clinical expert panel consisting of a psychiatrist, a neurologist and a psychologist, who reviewed neuroimaging scans (CT, MRI) when available, and also the results of three cognitive screenings tests

signalling.question: 3.2 Was a pre-specified or standard outcome definition used?
signalling.quote: In the case of MCI, Petersen’s criteria (Petersen et al., 1999), while for AD, internationally used guidelines (McKhann et al., 2011) were followed.

signalling.question: 3.3 Were predictors excluded from the outcome definition?
signalling.quote: the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE Folstein et al., 1975), the Clock Drawing Test (CDT Freedman et al., 1994) and the Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale – Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-Cog Rosen et al., 1984)

signalling.question: 3.4 Was the outcome defined and determined in a similar way for all participants?
signalling.quote: Demographic data (i.e. age and education) and the results of the MMSE, CDT and ADAS-Cog tests of the three subject groups.

signalling.question: 3.5 Was the outcome determined without knowledge of predictor information?
signalling.quote: MCI and mAD patients were selected after a medical diagnosis.

signalling.question: 3.6 Was the time interval between predictor assessment and outcome determination appropriate?
signalling.quote: Searched for the time between clinical diagnosis and speech recording; only found 'those having no cognitive impairment at the time of recording'.

domains.rationale: There are 25 participants per class against 51 to 151 features, and 75 were analysed from more than 150 recorded. No calibration is reported. Precision, recall, specificity and F1 use an Equal Error Rate threshold set on the evaluated predictions. Several feature, task and acoustic-model configurations were compared on the same cross-validation, and the best was headlined. Fusion weights are not specified, and there is no external validation. On the positive side, the split is by participant and the SVM C parameter is tuned by nested cross-validation.

signalling.quote: each speaker group, resulting in a total of 75 speakers and 225 recordings.

signalling.question: 4.2 Were continuous and categorical predictors handled appropriately?

signalling.question: 4.3 Were all enrolled participants included in the analysis?

signalling.question: 4.4 Were participants with missing data handled appropriately?

applicability.rationale: The sample is from a Hungarian memory clinic, with consensus-diagnosis cases only and demographically matched groups. Mild AD makes up one third of the sample, which is unlike an MCI screening population.
The speech tasks are feasible in practice, although the two recall tasks need a purpose-made film.
Standard clinical diagnoses of MCI and mild AD.

overall_rationale: Domains 1 and 4 are high: a diagnostic case-control sample that excluded contested diagnoses and was reduced by matching, and a very small development set (25 per class) with many features. There is also no calibration, a post hoc EER threshold, best-configuration selection on the same cross-validation, and no external validation.
